What it does

Model Composer builds a model from data. For a transistor it builds a nonlinear FET model, a .cmodel that a schematic places as a ComposedFET and that DC, S-parameters, harmonic balance and loadpull all use. For an N-port it builds a passive model, an ordinary cell of R, L, C and mutuals with the fitted values as its parameters.

The data can be measured (DC and pulsed I–V, multi-bias S-parameters, pulsed S-parameters, large-signal sweeps and loadpull) or simulated (tables of currents, admittances and intrinsic voltages written by another simulator). The work is kept in a .cmc document. It names the data where it lies, records the conditions it was measured under, and holds every setting and every result, so a model can be rebuilt, checked and changed later.

A transistor model has four parts, called constituents: the drain current Id, the gate current Ig (a gate–source and a gate–drain branch), and the gate and drain charges Qg and Qd. Each one is an ANN, a table or an equation. They sit inside an extrinsic network of pads, inductances and resistances. A model can add self-heating, trap states, or a simpler DC/RF dispersion. A .cmodel can also be written without the composer, from equations, a table or a network trained elsewhere: Writing a .cmodel.

Starting from another simulator's design kit? AN-04 — A nonlinear FET model from a reference kit walks the whole flow with block diagrams: which runs to make in the source simulator, the plane to sample at, what each step does with the result, and how to validate against the kit.

The steps

An active document runs through the steps below, in order. Each step's result is stored in the .cmc and stamped with the data and network it came from. When either changes, the step is marked stale.

Step What it does
Data Imports each data set and states its conditions. The data stays in its files and is cached beside the document.
Pads Removes the probe pads: open and short dummies, a Touchstone two-port per side, or a two-pin schematic per side.
Network Chooses the extrinsic network and fits its values. Every data set is then re-referenced to the intrinsic plane.
Current Fits Id and Ig.
Charge Fits Qg and Qd, or, with no S data, writes them from typed capacitances.
Thermal Adds self-heating: Rth (typed, or extracted from pulsed I–V) and the thermal time constants.
Traps Chooses a trap model and its coupling: fits the currents again with the trap states as inputs, or fits the strengths of a threshold shift from multi-bias S.
Check Checks that the charges conserve charge.
Validate Compares the model with every data set at the plane it was measured at.
Export Writes the .cmodel.

Fit all (model fit --step all) runs every step the document needs, in this order: the network if any value is free, then thermal, current, traps when a trap model is chosen, and charge. With no S data, the network is held at its values (network: held at its values — no S data to fit to) and the charge step writes the typed capacitances; a fit of the network step alone still refuses.

Data kinds and their conditions

Kind Holds Read from
DcIv Terminal voltages and currents at DC CSV, .mat, .npz, .npy
PulsedIv The same, sampled during a pulse from a stated quiescent point CSV, .mat, .npz, .npy
SParams Two-port S at each bias, and the bias currents when the files state them A folder of Touchstone files
PulsedSParams S sampled during a pulse A folder of Touchstone files
SimulatedTables Currents, and an admittance or S table, a capacitance table, or both; optionally intrinsic voltages .mat, .npz, .npy
LargeSignal A power sweep, a two-tone sweep or a loadpull file; used for validation only CSV, .spl, .lpcwave
PassiveSParams An N-port block, or a family of blocks over a geometry value Touchstone files

A Touchstone set takes its bias from each file's name or comment lines through a pattern such as Vgs{vgs}_Vds{vds}_Id{id:mA}. The fields are {vgs}, {vds}, {T}, {id}, {ig} and, for a passive family, {geometry}.

Each data set states the conditions it was measured under. Every condition is optional when the set is imported, and the step that needs one names it when it is missing.

Condition Meaning
AmbientC The chuck temperature, °C
ReferencePlane Where the bias voltages were measured: instrument, probe, device or intrinsic (below)
BiasPathOhms For instrument: the bias-path resistance at the gate, drain and source
Quiescent A pulsed set's quiescent bias (Vgs, Vds, and Id when it conducts)
PrePulse A double pulse's trap-setting pulse: its Vgs, Vds, width and gap before the measuring pulse
PulseWidth, Period, SampleDelay The pulse timing, seconds; the sample delay is from the pulse's start to the sample
TrapState How pulsed points beyond the trap-setting bias are used: auto, setting or extreme (below)
SoakTime, Compliance How long the bias was held, and the instrument's current limits
LargeSignal For a large-signal set: what it measured, the frequency, the bias and the terminations
Note Free text, kept with the set

Preparing the data

What data a model needs, how to sample it in another simulator, and the file formats each kind is read from — each with an example to copy — are on their own page: Model Data. It covers what a model needs, bias ranges and steps, running another simulator, the file formats, checking a file before importing it and what the import checks.

Reference planes

The composer always models in intrinsic voltages, between the core's own gate, drain and source. Each data set states the plane its voltages were measured at:

Plane Means
instrument At the source-measure unit; the bias-path resistances are subtracted
probe At the probe tips; the pads are removed, then the network
device Pads already removed; the network is removed
intrinsic Already intrinsic, as a simulator's tables can be

The intrinsic voltages come from a DC solve of the extrinsic network carrying the measured currents. Intrinsic points therefore do not lie on a grid, even when the measured ones do. ANNs train on them directly, and tables re-grid them.

A simulated table that also carries intrinsic voltages gets the computed ones checked against them. model deembed reports the largest difference, for example max |ΔV| 3.1e-10 V between its intrinsic voltages and the computed ones.

The six-pin network

The extrinsic network is an ordinary schematic with six numbered pins: 1, 2 and 3 are the extrinsic gate, drain and source, and 4, 5 and 6 are the intrinsic gate, drain and source. Pin 3 is the ground the data is referenced to. Each pin is numbered once. A network that breaks this rule is refused, and nothing is written.

The network's values are its variables. Each one can be locked, bounded, tied to another (rd × 1.2) and fitted. Three stock networks are provided: GaN two-shell (outer pad capacitances, inductances with a gate–drain mutual, inner capacitances, then the series resistances), classic single shell, and series only. The network is fitted cold-FET (a pinched-off and a forward-gate point), multi-bias (the intrinsic capacitances made flat in frequency at every chosen bias), or both. After a fit, each value has a standard error, and a value the data barely determines is marked with the partner it is correlated with.

Methods and their defaults

Setting Default
Method, every constituent ANN
ANN Two hidden layers of 8, tanh; 6000 iterations for a current, 3000 for a charge; 3 restarts; 10 % held out
Drain-current weighting Relative, with a floor at 10 % of the largest current (IdFloor 0.1)
Gate current Fitted as asinh(Ig/I0) with I0 at 1e-4 of the largest gate current (IgFloor); an equation Ig is fitted directly
Table Grid step 0.1 V; a charge table integrates along the mean of paths A and B
Charges An ANN trained on the capacitances alone (the adjoint method), anchored to zero charge at a stated bias
DC/RF dispersion Off; τ 1 µs when on
Self-heating Off
Traps None
Network fit Multi-bias

A model never extrapolates freely. Outside its training domain each constituent is continued linearly from the domain's edge. A current also gains a conductance on its own branch, which grows with distance from the edge: ten times the current's own conductance at the edge it leaves, capped at ten times its largest in the data. Where the data is flat, as a gate current below pinch-off, the continuation stays flat; where it is steep, as the forward gate diode, it stays steep. The Current step reports that conductance at each current's lowest and highest Vgs, as IgGs 2e-09 S at −6 V, 4.9 S at 1 V. The data is still the better answer: keep it wider than the voltages the circuit will reach, because beyond it the current is a continuation, not the device's.

How an ANN is trained

An ANN constituent is a small network, two hidden layers of 8 tanh neurons by default, trained by circuitRF's own trainer. It trains on two kinds of target, alone or together:

Target Trains
Values: the function itself at each bias Id and Ig, from the I–V data
Derivatives: the function's slope along vgs and vds Qg and Qd, from the capacitances; with self-heating, Id as well, from the RF Gm and Gds

The adjoint method for the charges

S-parameters do not measure a charge. They measure its derivatives: at each bias the intrinsic admittance gives the four capacitances C11 = ∂Qg/∂vgs, C12 = ∂Qg/∂vds, C21 = ∂Qd/∂vgs and C22 = ∂Qd/∂vds, averaged over the band where they are flat. An ANN charge is trained on those derivatives alone [P1 §6.3], [X03]:

  1. At each bias the network gives its value and its derivatives with respect to its inputs. The derivatives come from a second network carried forward with the first, so they are exact, never differenced.
  2. The loss is the weighted squared difference between those derivatives and the measured capacitances. For Qg it is (∂Qg/∂vgs − C11)² + (∂Qg/∂vds − C12)², summed over the biases.
  3. The loss's gradient with respect to every weight is back-propagated through both networks at once: the exact adjoint sensitivity of [X03]. An L-BFGS optimiser [NW06] minimises it.
  4. Derivatives fix a charge only up to a constant, so an anchor holds each charge at zero at one bias: (0, 0) by default, or the bias you state, moved to the nearest data point when it lies outside the data.

The result is one function per terminal, so the model conserves charge whatever the data. When the measured capacitances are not the derivatives of one function (their curl, which Check (a) reads, is not zero), the fit is the least-squares compromise between them [P1 §6.3.6], and Check (b) reads near zero on the model. A table charge takes the other route and integrates the capacitances along a path, so its result depends on the path [P1 §6.3]; the adjoint-trained ANN has no path.

A bias whose capacitances are not flat across the band weighs less: when the worse of C11's and C22's flatness exceeds FlatnessLimit (0.1), the point weighs (limit/flatness)². With S at two temperatures or more, an ANN charge takes T as a third input, and the anchor holds both charges at zero at every temperature, so heating moves no charge at the anchor bias [X10]. Drift charge in Qg splits the gate charge into depletion charges, fitted the same way to the capacitances near vds = 0, and a drift charge that follows Id [I11].

The currents

Id and Ig train on the measured values, Id weighted relative to the current with a floor (IdFloor). With self-heating, Id also trains on derivatives: the I–V values at each point's junction temperature, and each S point's RF Gm and Gds as ∂Id/∂vgs and ∂Id/∂vds at the same point [X03], [X10]. One function then gives both the DC and the RF output conductance [P1 §6.6]. With the current step's Symmetry set to Exchange in the .cmc, the currents are defined for vds ≥ 0 only, and at negative vds they are their own image with drain and source exchanged [P1 §6.5], [X07]. It is off by default, because a field-plated power device is asymmetric by design.

Common to every ANN

  • Each input is scaled onto [−1, 1] over the training points, and the output onto the same range, so one network size suits a 10 mA device and a 10 A one.
  • Restarts (3 by default) start from different seeded weights, and the start with the lowest held-out error is kept. The same data, settings and seed give the same model, to the bit, on every machine.
  • Held out (10 % by default) are spread across the bias plane rather than taken from one corner, and the status strip's held-out error is the model's error on them.
  • Iterations cap the optimiser. It stops sooner when the loss stops falling.
  • A network with more weights than a tenth of its targets says so in one line: it can fit the noise.

Charge conservation

The charges are charge functions, so a model is charge-conserving by construction. Its capacitances are derivatives of one charge each, and no DC is ever made by displacement current. Check Charge Conservation checks three things:

Check Reads A good result
(a) The data The curl of the measured capacitance matrix, row by row, and the difference between the two line-integral paths A few percent: the data's own noise and the network's error
(b) The model The same curl on the fitted model's capacitances Near zero
(c) Large signal A harmonic-balance drive at f and at 2f; the change in DC gate current is DC made by displacement current Below 0.1 % of the fundamental gate current

Check (a) needs S at 4 biases or more across the bias plane; with fewer it reports not run and the number of biases, which is not a failure. With typed charges it reports not run, as there is no S data. A linear or typed charge's (b) reads zero.

A non-reciprocal capacitance matrix (a transcapacitance, C21 ≠ C12) is reported for information. It is physical, and it is not an error. Checks (b) and (c) also run on any nonlinear device in a netlist: model check-charge design.cnl --device X1 --bias vgs,vds.

Temperature

Data at two or more temperatures makes T an input of every constituent. The model then follows the run's ambient temp, clamped to the data's range with one warning, and self-heating is available. An equation template's current scale (Ipk, Beta or Idss) is then linear in T unless you say otherwise; see the method picker.

Data at one temperature makes a model valid at that temperature, T0, with no temperature dependence. Self-heating is unavailable. A run at another temp prints one warning naming both temperatures and uses the model as it is.

Self-heating needs an Rth. Type it, or extract it from pulsed I–V at two or more chuck temperatures, pulsed from a quiescent point that dissipates nothing, together with DC I–V at the same biases. Extraction trains an isothermal current on the pulses, finds the junction temperature at which it gives each DC point's current, and fits the rise against the dissipated power. The thermal dynamics are a typed Cth, a typed τth, a Foster ladder, or τth fitted to the low-frequency roll-off of Re Y22. That fit is not offered while traps are modelled, because the roll-off holds trap time constants too.

When drain lag is modelled, type Rth (from a thermal simulation, for example) rather than extract it. A pulse from a 0 V drain leaves the trap state short of its DC value, and extraction reads that shortfall as heating.

Traps, and what pulsed data allows

Traps are a setting. None is the default. CaptureEmission has a gate-lag state and a drain-lag state, each switched on separately. A state is captured quickly when its voltage moves one way and emits slowly when it moves back. The defaults are 10 ns capture at a 1 V gap and 1 ms emission, and emission can be made thermally activated. Custom lets you write each state's dynamics and DC value yourself.

The coupling says how the states reach the drain current:

Coupling The current Needs
Trained (the default with pulsed I–V) Id takes the enabled states as inputs and is fitted again with them Pulsed I–V
Shift Id is the trap-free current fitted to the DC I–V, evaluated at a shifted gate voltage: Id(vgs − ΔV, vds), with ΔV = ShiftDrain·(φ2 − vds) + ShiftGate·(vgs − φ1) Nothing beyond DC I–V; multi-bias S to fit the strengths

Under Shift a drain-lag state held above vds, or a gate-lag state held below vgs, lowers the current. At any DC bias every state equals its DC value, so the shift is zero and the model's DC is exactly the trap-free current. At RF the states are frozen, which gives gm_RF = (1 − ShiftGate)·gm and gds_RF = gds + ShiftDrain·gm, where gm and gds are the trap-free current's. The step fits each strength from these relations over the active S biases. A strength can be typed and locked, and is then not fitted. The time constants are typed in both couplings. Shift is defined for CaptureEmission; the charges take no trap state under it. With self-heating modelled, gm and gds are read at each point's junction temperature, so heating is not counted as traps. Without self-heating, ShiftDrain includes any thermal part of the DC/RF difference.

A trained trap state is fitted from the trap-setting levels in the pulsed data. The level of a set is its pre-pulse bias for a double pulse, and its quiescent bias otherwise.

Pulsed data What it allows
Double pulse The pre-pulse sets the state, and the measuring pulse reads it before emission moves it. This is the clearest data.
Ordinary pulses from two or more quiescent points Two or more levels: the state is fitted fully.
One quiescent point One level: the state is fitted with one warning, and the model records the level it came from.
No pulsed data Threshold-shift traps, time constants typed, strengths typed or fitted from multi-bias S.

A pulsed point toward its setting (pulsed no higher in Vds for drain lag, no lower in Vgs for gate lag) sits at the setting's state exactly, because only slow emission acted. A point beyond it was partly captured during the pulse. The set's TrapState decides what happens to it: auto keeps it for validation only, setting takes the setting's state, and extreme takes the pulse's own voltage as the state.

DC/RF dispersion is the simpler alternative to traps. It fits a second drain current, IdRF, to the RF transconductance and output conductance, and the model follows Id at DC and IdRF above the corner set by τ. Dispersion and traps are not combined, in either coupling.

Periphery scaling

A model records the measured device's finger count N0 and unit gate width W0. Export needs both. An instance's N scales the model:

What Scales by
The core (Id, Ig, Qg, Qd) N/N0
A network value, by its rule fixed, perFinger (N/N0) or perFingerInverse (N0/N)
Rth, Cth N0/N, N/N0
Trap time constants Not scaled

For the GaN two-shell network the series resistances are perFingerInverse, the inner capacitances perFinger, and the pad capacitances, inductances and mutual fixed. Every rule can be changed per value. m places whole devices in parallel, so m=2 N=8 is two 8-finger devices.

Passive models

A passive document holds one N-port block, or a family of blocks over a geometry value such as the turns of a spiral. Analyse reports the block's reciprocity, passivity, symmetry, low-frequency asymptotes and self-resonances, and fits a rational model. Propose ranks a library of twelve topologies (series and parallel RLC, an inductor with skin effect, capacitor and resistor parasitics, π, T, bond wire, via, spiral, MIM and a line with pads) against the data, or fits a topology you draw. Fit gives each value with its error.

A family is fitted as one law per value, a polynomial or a rational function of the geometry. The middle geometry is held out and predicted, and the result reports its error. Export writes a cell. A single fit's cell takes the fitted values as its parameters, each in the unit that keeps it between 1 and 1000 (nH, fF, Ω). A family cell takes the geometry as its only parameter: the element values stay variables on the cell's schematic, each a law of the geometry — x is the geometry normalised to the fitted range and every law a short polynomial or ratio in it — and the cell warns once when it is placed outside the fitted range.

The example

File ▸ New ▸ Examples ▸ Model Composer opens a workspace with three documents built this way:

  • synthetic-gan: a GaN FET built from synthetic DC, pulsed and multi-bias S data, with a fitted network, ANN currents, adjoint-ANN charges, self-heating and drain lag. Its 8-finger model drives a class-AB power sweep and a loadpull.
  • passive-spiral: a family of spiral inductors over turns, fitted and placed in a filter at a turn count between two measured ones.
  • simulated-tables: a model built from a simulator's tables, showing the intrinsic-voltage cross-check.

The synthetic-gan model is also there as Verilog-A source, gan_4x125.va, and the GanVerilogA bench runs the two side by side: Verilog-A export.

Its README lists every setting it uses, and the value a real job would use where it differs.

Opening a document

Tools ▸ Model Composer… opens a window on a new document and asks one question: Active (a three-terminal FET) or Passive (an N-port). Nothing is written until the first save, which asks where the .cmc goes; choosing a network saves first, because the document's data and network files are found relative to it. Importing data into a new document asks for the data first, then opens the Save dialog in the data's folder with the first file's name filled in, since the data is kept beside the .cmc. Cancelling that Save imports nothing.

A .cmc in a workspace opens on double-click in the project tree, and the window's Open button opens one from anywhere. Each document has one window; opening a document that is already open brings its window forward.

Closing a window with unsaved work asks whether to save it. A document is reopened where it was left: the same panels, the same step, and the same bias cursor.

An opened document needs nothing run to be looked at: its data opens and every step that has a result draws it. The step rail marks each finished step ✓, and the status strip says what is there, e.g. 8 data sets open · done: Pads, Network, Current, Charge, Thermal, Traps, Export. Run re-runs the selected step; on the Data step, with data already imported, it reloads that data, and Import… is on the ▾ and beside the data-set list.

The window

Part What it holds
Toolbar Open, Save, Save As · Undo, Redo · the four panel lamps · Check Charge Conservation, Model Validation Report · Run ▾, Cancel · Help
Steps (left) The step rail, and under it the selected step's settings
Plots (centre) A tab strip; under it the bias cursor (Vgs, Vds, T, Q) or the model sweep, whichever the plot reads; and a Data Display plot
Network (right, top) The extrinsic network, drawn by the schematic canvas
Values (right, bottom) The network's values: value, lock, min, max, tie, scaling rule, ± error. Widening the panel widens the name column only; narrower than its columns, the table scrolls sideways
Status strip One line — a result, a warning or a refusal — and, while something runs, its stage, a progress bar and Cancel

Panel lamps. Each panel has a lamp on the toolbar; a lit lamp means the panel is on screen. Hiding a panel gives its space to the others. The last lit lamp cannot be turned off. Which panels are hidden is saved in the document. The splitters between panels drag in both directions.

The step rail. Active documents have Data · Pads · Network · Current · Charge · Thermal · Traps · Check · Validate · Export; passive ones have Data · Topology · Fit · Export. A step that cannot run yet is dimmed and its tooltip says what it needs. A ✓ marks a step whose result the document holds; a dot instead marks a result computed before the data, the network or the trap model last changed. Check and Validate keep no result in the document, so they are marked once run.

The bias cursor. Vgs, Vds, the ambient temperature and the quiescent point. Each list holds only measured values, so the cursor always sits on a measured bias; with a list focused, the arrow keys step it. The lists sit under the plot tabs, beside the plot they set. Every frequency plot is drawn at the measured point nearest the cursor. A list shows only on the plot tabs that read it: Vgs and Vds on the frequency plots, the bias plane and the Gm, Gds and pulsed slices; T and Q where a step's plot picks a data set by them, which is when the data-set list's selection is not one of that step's sets.

The model sweep. On the tabs that evaluate a fitted model rather than show data at a measured bias — the Current step's Model tabs and the Charge step's C–V tabs — the row under the plot tabs holds start, stop and step for vgs and for vds instead, in volts. A value takes effect on Return or on leaving its box; Escape puts back the one it had. Both are intrinsic, the plane the model is fitted on. One voltage is the x axis and the other steps the curves; the x-axis voltage is drawn at its step or at 101 points, whichever is finer. The sweep starts from the step's data span and keeps what you type for the rest of the session; it is not saved in the document.

Running, progress and Cancel

Run runs the selected step's main task, which its tooltip names; the ▾ beside it lists the step's others. Every run happens off the user interface, which stays responsive: the status strip shows the stage — which network is training, Training Ig, start 2 of 3 — and one progress bar, and Cancel stops it.

  • One task runs at a time. Starting another while one runs is refused in the status strip.
  • A cancelled task changes nothing: the previous result stays exactly as it was.
  • A run that changes results (an import, a fit) saves the document first and reads the result back; an edit made while it ran is kept on top of the result.

The Data step

Import (the database button, or Run) opens the importer:

Field Meaning
Kind DC I–V, pulsed I–V, S-parameters, pulsed S-parameters, simulated tables, large signal
Source Files, or a folder — a Touchstone set is a folder of files
Pattern Touchstone: how each file name (or its comments) states its bias, e.g. Vgs{vgs}_Vds{vds}_Id{id:mA}
Map CSV, .mat, .npz, .npy: what each column or array holds, name=quantity[:unit]. For an array file it is filled in from the array names
Conditions Ambient °C, the reference plane, the quiescent point, and any other condition as Key=Value

The right side previews the first lines of the first file — for an array file, each array it holds with its shape — and the first points as they will be read; the line at the bottom is what the import will read, how it read any array not in the documented layout, or why it cannot.

The data-set list shows each set's name, kind, ambient, reference plane, quiescent point (and pre-pulse) and point count, and where its charges read their capacitances: Y, its capacitance table or its circuit set. circuitrf model explain says the same. A capacitance table spelled as the matrix whose C12 is positive at most of its points is warned about, since the matrix convention has C12 = −Cgd: the circuit set was probably meant. Selecting a set points the plots and the cursor's lists at it.

Under the list, an active document shows what its data supports, one row per kind of data in the table of what a model needs: I–V, S or capacitances, cold-FET S, two or more temperatures, pulsed data and large-signal runs. A lit row says what that data gives the model; a dim one says what would light it, in the words the step rail uses for a step that cannot open yet, so the two never disagree.

Plot tab Shows
Output Id against Vds, one curve per Vgs; excluded points as ×
Transfer Id against Vgs, one curve per Vds
Bias plane Every bias point: extrinsic ○, intrinsic ●, excluded ×, hygiene flags ▲, the cursor a green dot
S The four S-parameters in dB at the cursor's bias
Smith S11 and S22 at the cursor's bias

Moving the cursor. On the bias plane, with the lasso lamp off, click a point: it turns green, the Vgs and Vds lists move to its bias, and the other tabs follow. A plot you have zoomed or panned keeps its window while the cursor moves; choosing another tab frames that tab's data. A point of another data set selects that set.

Excluding points. On the bias plane, light the lasso lamp under the plot tabs, choose a reason, then click a point or drag a lasso around several. Points already excluded are included again. Choose Valid instead to make every point the click or lasso takes valid again, excluded or not. Each click or lasso is one undo step.

To take a group of points out of the fit:

  1. On the Data step, choose the Bias plane tab (the grid of dots).
  2. Light the lasso lamp, the third button under the tabs. The reason list beside it is enabled.
  3. Choose why the points are going: Outlier, Oscillation, Compliance, Drift, Breakdown or Other. The reason is kept with each point in the .cmc.
  4. Drag a loop round the points. Releasing the button closes the loop and excludes every point inside it; each is drawn with a ×. A single click excludes the nearest point.
  5. Turn the lasso lamp off again to go back to moving the cursor with a click.

Every fit after that leaves the excluded points out. To put one back, lasso or click it again, or choose Valid and lasso a whole region. Undo takes back one lasso at a time.

Base periphery. N0 (fingers) and W0 (unit gate width, with its unit, e.g. 125 um) of the measured device. Export needs them; until they are set the Data step shows the one warning that says so.

The Pads step

The pad mode — None, OpenShort, TwoPorts or Network — and its files. The S and Smith tabs show S at the cursor's bias before (dashed) and after (solid) the pads come off.

The Network step

The network. The book button picks a stock network (GaN two-shell, classic single shell, series only) or none; the folder button opens a six-pin .csch; the pencil opens the network in the schematic editor. Copy puts the network on the clipboard as a schematic selection that pastes into any schematic; Paste takes a selection from a schematic as the network. A network whose pins are not numbered 1 to 6, each once, is refused in one line, and nothing is written.

The values table. Every value is editable: type a value with or without its unit (39.5 pH, 39.5p), tick the lock to hold it, set a minimum and a maximum, tie it to another value (rd or rd × 1.2), and choose its scaling rule. After a fit, ± is each value's standard error, and ⚠ marks a poorly determined value — its tooltip names the correlated partner or the bound it sits at.

The fit. Method (ColdFet, MultiBias, ColdFetThenMultiBias, or Fixed, which holds every value), seed and the three weights. The multi-bias fit's bias points are marked ■ on the bias plane; with the lasso lamp lit on the Network step a click or lasso adds points to that set or takes them out.

Plot tab Shows
C Intrinsic Cgs, Cgd and Cds against frequency at the cursor's bias, in fF
G Intrinsic Gm and Gds against frequency, in mS
Flatness The flatness of Cgs, Cgd and Cds across bias, one curve per Vds, in %
Bias plane As on the Data step, with the fit's points

A right network leaves C and G flat in frequency.

The method picker

The Current and Charge steps pick a method for each constituent with the same control:

Method Settings
ANN Hidden layers (1 to 4, neurons each, default 8, 8), activation, iterations. A charge needs S at 4 biases or more
Table Grid step and smoothing; a charge table also takes its line-integral path — A, B or their mean. A charge needs S at 4 biases or more
Equation A template, or Custom for your own expression in vgs, vds and named parameters; after a fit, each parameter's value, which can be selected and copied. A charge needs at least as many capacitances as free parameters, two per bias, so Linear fits from one

Choosing Equation starts on the first template. A template shows the law it fits; the expression boxes are Custom's. Linear in T names the current template's parameters made linear in temperature, p + p_T·(T − Tnom). Left blank it is the template's current scale (Ipk for Angelov, Beta for Curtice and Statz, Idss for Materka) when the data spans temperatures, so that hot DC points and cooler pulsed points are not fitted by one law; none turns it off.

With fewer S biases than a method needs, its entry in the picker gives the reason when you hover over it, and a fit with it is refused rather than run with another method.

A table on gridded data is the data. When a constituent's training points form a complete grid in its inputs, every combination present once, as intrinsic-plane simulated tables do, the table is a spline through the samples themselves on that grid: no re-grid, and the Re-grid setting is not read. Its held-out points are whole grid lines along vgs, so the rest stay a grid. A charge table does the same with capacitances on a grid. A grid with a missing site, an excluded point for one, is re-gridded, and the report names the sites missing.

Otherwise a table samples a smooth function of the points onto its grid: an ANN trained on them (the default) or a radial-basis interpolant through them (RBF). The RBF solves one dense system over every point, so its memory grows with the square of the point count and its time with the cube: about 11 s at 4,000 points and 22 s at 5,000. Above 5,000 points a fit with it is refused before it starts; re-grid through the ANN.

Restarts, the seed and the held-out percentage belong to the step. After a fit the status strip reads, for example, Id: ANN 2×8 · held-out 0.8 % · domain 412 pts. An ANN Id whose held-out error passes 2 % of its range over more than 2,000 training points adds the next size up: 2×8 under-fits 24,000 points: try 2×16, or a Table.

The Current step

Pickers for Id and Ig — an equation Ig is two expressions, IgGs and IgGd — and DC/RF dispersion, the simpler alternative to self-heating and traps. Id floor and Ig floor, under the pickers, are the document's IdFloor and IgFloor, each a fraction of the largest current: Id is weighted by 1/max(|Id|, floor)², so a lower floor fits subthreshold current more closely, and Ig is fitted as asinh(Ig/I0) with I0 the gate floor.

Plot tab Shows
Output, Transfer Measured Id (symbols) and the model (lines), one member per measured Vgs or Vds, at the cursor's temperature and quiescent point
Model (vds), Model (vgs) The fitted Id over the model sweep — along vds with a curve per vgs, or the reverse — at the cursor's temperature, every trap state at its DC value. Beyond the training domain the model's continuation is dashed and left out of the autoscale
Error Model minus data over the bias plane, in % of the current's range
Gm, Gds The data's own derivative (symbols) against the model, at the cursor's Vds or Vgs; with dispersion, RF Gm and Gds from the S data as well
Domain The training points and the outline of the domain beyond which the model extrapolates

The Charge step

Pickers for Qg and Qd (an adjoint-trained ANN by default, a table integrated along a path, or an equation), and Drift charge in Qg. The charge templates are Depletion, Angelov and Linear.

Linear is Qg = C11·vgs + C12·vds and Qd = C21·vgs + C22·vds: constant capacitances, exact at a single measured bias. From two or three biases it is the least-squares constant matrix, and the report gives each value's spread across the biases, with the circuit set Cgs = C11 + C12, Cgd = −C12, Cds = C22 + C12 and Cm = C21 − C12. Its C–V plots are flat lines through the measured points. The exported model's provenance and circuitrf model explain say Qg, Qd: Linear from 1 bias point(s). A linear charge has no training domain, so no extrapolation applies to it.

With no S, Y or capacitance data, the step shows four capacitances in place of the pickers — Cgs, Cgd, Cds and Cm, each in farads and 0 unless you type a value — and Run writes them as Linear charges. A datasheet gives them as Cgd = Crss, Cgs = Ciss − Crss and Cds = Coss − Crss; Cm is a transcapacitance and may be negative. Export, the provenance and circuitrf model explain say Qg, Qd: typed with the four values. With all four at zero the step, the export and model explain say the charges are zero: S-parameters and harmonic balance see the currents alone. — a model meant only for DC. Validation then has DC and large-signal items and no S items. Typed values beside S data are refused, since typing would discard the data; Fit to the S data clears them.

Plot tab Shows
C–V (vgs), C–V (vds) The model's capacitances along one voltage over the model sweep's span, a curve per value of the other voltage that the sweep steps, measured points near each as symbols. The selector beside the tabs picks one Cij or the circuit set Cgs, Cgd, Cds, Cm
Qg, Qd The model's charge over (vds, vgs)
ΔQg, ΔQd The model's charge against the line integral of the measured capacitances, in % of the charge's range

The Thermal step

Self-heating, Rth (blank extracts it), Cth or a ladder of fraction:τ pairs; Extract (Run) runs the extraction and the line under the settings gives its Rth and residual. A document whose data is at one temperature shows its T0 and the words one temperature instead: the model it builds has no temperature dependence.

Plot tab Shows
Tj Each DC point's junction-temperature rise against its dissipated power, and the model's Rth line
DC I–V Measured Id, the model with self-heating (solid) and the isothermal model (dashed)

The Traps step

The trap model (None, CaptureEmission, Custom), its coupling, a toggle per state, the time constants, and for Custom each state's dynamics and DC expressions with the result of the fixed-point check. A state the data cannot support shows why in place of its toggle; a state trained from one trap-setting level shows that level. Without pulsed I–V the coupling list holds Shift only, and one line under it says why. Under Shift, each enabled state's strength has a lock, its value and, after a fit, its ± standard error. Typing a value locks it. The step's report gives each strength and the RMS residual of both relations.

Choosing a model, or None, changes what the currents must be trained with, so the step is marked stale until it runs and Export waits for it. None with currents trained with traps: Run re-trains Id and Ig without them, on the DC data — the pulsed sets are left out, and the report says so. None with trap-free currents: there is nothing to run, and the step is never stale, since nothing reads an earlier trap fit. Shift with currents trained with traps: Run re-trains them trap-free first, then fits the strengths.

Plot tab Shows
Pulsed I–V Trained: per trap-setting level, measured Id against the model at the cursor's Vgs; points pulsed beyond the trap-setting bias are hollow — validation only
DC I–V Trained: the DC data against the model, as validation
Gm Shift: Gm against Vgs at the cursor's Vds — RF from S (symbols), the shifted model with its states frozen (lines), the trap-free current (dashed)
Gds Shift: Gds against Vds at the cursor's Vgs, drawn the same way

The Check step

Check Charge Conservation — also on the toolbar — checks the data, the fitted model and a large-signal drive. The result is one row each — Data gate 0.40 %, Data drain 3.80 %, Model < 0.01 %, HB 0.2 µA — and the transcapacitance as information. A percentage below 0.01 % reads < 0.01 %: a residual that small is zero for this purpose.

Plot tab Shows
Curl Qg, Curl Qd Each charge row's curl over the bias plane, %
Paths Qg, Paths Qd The two line-integral paths' difference, % of the charge's range
Spectrum The gate current's spectrum with the drive at f and at 2f; a change in its DC is DC made by a non-conservative charge

The Validate step

One row per data set with its tolerance and, after a run, its result line. Run all, or ▶ on one row. The tolerances are edited below the rows.

A loadpull file is compared at compression, not drive by drive: at each load the measurement drives to the Compression setting (3 dB of Gt by default), the model is driven to the same compression at that load, and Pout, Gt, PAE, drain efficiency and AM/PM are compared there, with Zin as the VSWR between measured and model. Each side's own MXP and MXE are compared too, by their Pout or efficiency and by their load, as a VSWR. Only what the file carries is compared, and only at loads the measurement drives that far; a file that reaches the compression at no load says so and is not graded. circuitrf model validate --compression 2 changes it for one run. Show testbench writes each item's generated .cnl beside the .cmc and shows it in the file manager.

Plot tab Shows
S, Smith S at the measurement plane at the cursor's bias, measured (symbols) against model (lines)
I–V The I–V family
Power, IM Pout, gain, PAE and Id, or IM3 and IM5, against input power
Loadpull Measured and modelled Pout contours at the compression the comparison is made at

The Model Validation Report

Model Validation Report… (toolbar, or the Validate step) opens a dialog with every option of the report. Each opens on the value stored in the document or its default; Apply stores them.

Option What it sets
Sections Which sections the report writes: DC I–V, Thermal, Charge, C–V, S and the PA classes. Leaving one out skips its runs too, and the PA classes are the slow one
S compared at these biases The biases whose S-parameters are compared, model against data. None ticked: the lowest, middle and highest current
C–V curves at Vds, at Vgs The fixed voltage of each C–V curve. None chosen: five spread over the data
PA classes Which classes (B, J, J*, F, F⁻¹) are loadpulled with the model, and at what frequency and bias
R_opt, Source Z, Source 2f0 The optimum load resistance and the source's fundamental and second-harmonic terminations. Empty: from the knee, a conjugate match, and a short
Radius, rings, spokes The disc of loads round each class's optimum: its reflection-coefficient radius, and how finely it is sampled
Drive start, step, max The input-power ladder each load is driven up, in dBm
Compression How far into compression each load is driven before its performance is read, in dB

Generate stores the options as Apply does, then runs and writes the report; Export PDF… writes it as one PDF. Closing the dialog without either leaves the document's options as they were.

The choices are the data's own values. The S biases are boxes laid out as the bias plane, Vds across and Vgs down; hover over one for its bias, tick the ones to compare. A very irregular plan, which would need more than 2,500 boxes, is typed instead. The C–V voltages are buttons, one per measured voltage, typed past 24. Beside each heading, Select all and Clear all tick or clear every value at once. Under each is how many are chosen, or what none chosen means: the lowest, middle and highest current for S, five voltages spread over the data for C–V. The frequency and the PA bias list the measured values and accept any other; left empty, each shows the value the report will use, such as the S data's median frequency.

Generate writes the report into <name>-report/ beside the .cmc, and its Data Display document, <name>-report.cdd, beside that folder: one tab per section — the bias points of every data set, I–V families, the ΔQ maps, the C–V families with the fixed voltage as the legend, S at the chosen biases, the Rth plot, and per PA class its loadpull contours, its performance table and the region where the drive-up converged. Export PDF… writes the report: its summary first, then every tab as a page headed by the conditions that reproduce it. model report --pdf writes the same file.

The summary is written for whoever uses the model in a design, who may not be whoever built it:

  • Scorecard. One row per test, each Green (very good to excellent), Yellow (usable, with something specific the designer should know) or Red (does not reasonably match the measurement, or does not converge), and what that means for a design. A comparison with data is Green within the validation's tolerance, Yellow within twice it, and Red beyond; points where the solve failed make it Yellow (up to 5 % of them) or Red. Rth is Green within 10 % of the data's and Yellow within 25 %; a charge within 2 % and 5 % of its range; a PA class when HB converges at its load and over 95 % (Yellow: 75 %) of the disc about it. The overall grade is the worst row.
  • Where the model is supported by data: the bias range the currents and charges were trained over, the hottest point in the I–V data, the temperatures, the frequencies checked, whether large-signal data was compared, and what the model does outside that range.
  • How the model was fitted: each current and charge as an equation (and which), a table (and its grid) or a neural network (and its layers), with its error on held-out points; traps, self-heating and the extrinsic network.
  • Data: every data set, what it was used for, its points and bias values, its temperatures and frequencies.

Each test's page states its bias, source and load terminations at every harmonic, frequency, temperature, Rth, and the harmonic count, tolerance, FFT oversample and iteration cap of the simulation, and names its testbench in testbenches/, which circuitrf dc, sparam, hb or lp runs as written. The same text is in summary.txt, and in report.json for a program to read.

The Export step

N0 and W0, which can be changed here as on the Data step, the scaling rule of each network value (the same rule as the Values table's scaling column, so either can set it), the symbol, and the .cmodel's path. The symbol shows as one picture; click it for the menu of every symbol the model can take, which are those with gate, drain and source pins (and a fourth for the thermal node of a self-heating model). The step's buttons are on its header: Export writes the model; Copy Instance puts an instance of it on the clipboard, ready to paste into a schematic; VA is Export Verilog-A. The plots show the model's Output and Transfer curves against its data. A placed instance's thermal pin T, and how to get it, is in The thermal pin, T.

A step whose result predates the data or the network blocks Export with one line naming it; Run stale re-runs the stale steps in order.

VA (Export Verilog-A…) writes the same model as Verilog-A source, for another simulator: Verilog-A export.

A placed model can have parts of itself switched off per instance, to see what each costs the circuit: Switching parts of the model off.

A passive document exports as a cell: its name, the library or workspace folder it goes in, and the fitted values as its parameters.

Switching parts of the model off

Ten instance switches turn one effect off on one ComposedFET, so you can see what it costs the circuit in gain, efficiency or linearity:

Switch Default What changes
Charge true false: the intrinsic device has no capacitance at all. The network's capacitors stay.
LinearC false true: the intrinsic capacitances are held at their values at the bias point, so they do not change with drive.
LinearCgs false true: Cgs alone is held at its bias-point value; the other capacitances follow the model.
LinearCdg false true: Cdg alone is held at its bias-point value.
LinearCds false true: Cds alone is held at its bias-point value.
LinearCm false true: the transcapacitance Cm alone is held at its bias-point value.
GateLag true false: gate-lag traps follow the voltage instantly.
DrainLag true false: drain-lag traps follow the voltage instantly.
SelfHeating true false: the device stays at the run's temp; pin 4, if wired, sees no rise.
Dispersion true false: the drain carries its DC current at every frequency.

Charge=false wins over every Linear switch, and LinearC=true is all four branch switches at once. Nothing refits: the .cmodel is untouched, and a switch changes only how that one instance evaluates it. A switch naming a part the model does not have — GateLag=false on a model with no gate-lag trap — changes nothing and says so, so one schematic can hold different models.

The bias point is the instance's quiescent DC operating point: the intrinsic vgs and vds of the circuit's own DC solution with every RF source at zero, with the junction temperature and trap states that solution has. Every analysis solves it first, and solves it again when a sweep moves the bias. With LinearC=true the charge is the tangent there, its temperature and trap inputs held too, so the capacitance is constant; the currents stay nonlinear. S-parameters at the bias point are therefore identical either way, and a power sweep differs only once the drive is large.

One capacitance at a time. The intrinsic device's charges are two terminal charges, Qg and Qd, not separate capacitors. Its capacitances are read from their derivatives, C11 = ∂Qg/∂vgs, C12 = ∂Qg/∂vds, C21 = ∂Qd/∂vgs and C22 = ∂Qd/∂vds, as the circuit set

Cgs = C11 + C12     Cdg = −C12     Cds = C22 + C12     Cm = C21 − C12

so Cgs sits between gate and source, Cdg between gate and drain, Cds between drain and source, and Cm is the drain charge's extra dependence on vgs. "Linear Cgs" means Cgs keeps its bias-point value at every voltage while Cdg, Cds and Cm follow the model. The charges stay charges, so nothing is lost or created over an RF cycle. At the bias point the device is exactly the model, so S-parameters there do not change. Once the drive is large, the difference shows which capacitance causes how much AM–PM and harmonic content. Any combination works: LinearCgs=true LinearCds=true holds both. With any of them set, the whole charge is read at the bias point's temperature and trap state, as LinearC does.

No gate lag means the trap state takes, at every instant, the value it would have at DC at those voltages. That trap then no longer tells RF from DC: the drain current under drive is the DC I–V surface in that respect, and a threshold shift from that trap is zero. Its node is not created.

Each switch is an ordinary parameter, so it can be bound to a variable and swept. To compare two runs on one plot:

gl = 1
ComposedFET:X1  g d s  File="gan_8x125.cmodel"  GateLag=gl
analysis HB1 type=hb Tone=2 GHz MaxHarm=5
analysis SW1 type=parametric_sweep Var=gl Values=1,0 Inner=HB1

In the schematic they are the Model switches group of the instance's parameters. An instance with any switch off carries one line under it naming what is off — linear C · no gate lag · isothermal, or linear Cgs, Cds — and every run that uses it adds one note to Messages. circuitrf explain reports each instance's switches.

In harmonicaRF

A .cmodel can be harmonicaRF's device. There the switches are checkboxes on the readout strip, and each toggle re-solves the loadline, the contours and the power sweep while you watch. The strip's DUT line names whatever is switched off. The loadline and its DCIV family are read at the intrinsic device, inside the network, with each DC curve at its own trap state and self-heated temperature.

Verilog-A export

VA (Export Verilog-A…) on the Export step's header writes the model as one Verilog-A source file, so the same model runs in another simulator. It asks where the file goes, offering <name>.va beside the .cmodel's path, and the line under the step's header names the file and its module. The file is self-contained: it includes only the standard disciplines and constants headers, and its header comment lists every parameter with its unit, default and meaning.

circuitRF runs Verilog-A too, so it can check the file itself. In the example, the GanVerilogA bench places the .cmodel as a ComposedFET and gan_4x125.va as a VerilogA on identical bias networks — ports 1 and 2 for one, 3 and 4 for the other — with a DC sweep, S-parameters and a drive sweep; its measures show each pair side by side. Running it needs a Verilog-A compiler (The compiler, and why it is yours).

Headless, the same function is circuitrf model export gan.cmc -o gan.va, and a .cmodel someone sent you exports with no document: circuitrf model export gan.cmodel -o gan.va (model).

What is exported

Everything a placed ComposedFET has: the network, the equation and ANN constituents, the continuation outside the training domain, drain–source symmetry, the charges, dispersion, the trap states, self-heating, the temperature range and periphery scaling. Equations and ANNs are written as code, so the file computes the model's own numbers.

Tables are not exported. A model with a table constituent shows one line on the Export step — Id and Qg are tables; Verilog-A export needs ANN or equation constituents. — and VA stays off; Export is unaffected. To export, refit that constituent as an ANN or an equation on its step (The method picker), then export again.

Terminals

g, d and s, and for a self-heating model a fourth, t, whose temperature is the channel's rise above the ambient, in K. Leave t off the symbol (one pin fewer) and the device heats on the model's own thermal network. Drawn and left unwired, it does the same: unlike the general rule in The thermal terminal, this module keeps its thermal network on a node of its own and joins t to it, so an unwired t is never a floating node. A thermal network wired to t sits in parallel with the model's, as on a ComposedFET's T pin.

Parameters

Parameter What it is
N The finger count. Currents, charges and network values scale from the measured device's N0, as on a ComposedFET.
Temp The device temperature, °C. Unset follows the simulator's.
Rth, Cth This device's own thermal resistance and capacitance at N fingers. Unset is the model's, scaled.
The ten switches Below.
VgsQ, VdsQ, TjQ The bias point the linear-charge switches hold the charge at. Below.
Network values One per value of the six-pin network, at its fitted value, with its scaling rule in the header.
Id_beta, … An equation constituent's parameters, named after the constituent.
Gx_Id, … The conductances the continuation outside the training domain adds.
Trap parameters The trap model's own, such as TauEmit2.

m is the host simulator's own device multiplier: it multiplies the whole device, so the module declares none.

The switches are those of Switching parts of the model off, as integers, 1 on and 0 off:

Switch Default 0 or 1 does
Charge 1 0: no intrinsic capacitance.
LinearC 0 1: the intrinsic capacitances held at the bias point.
LinearCgs, LinearCdg, LinearCds, LinearCm 0 1: that one capacitance held at the bias point.
GateLag, DrainLag 1 0: those trap states follow the voltage instantly.
SelfHeating 1 0: the device stays at Temp.
Dispersion 1 0: the drain carries its DC current at every frequency.

A switch naming a part the model does not have changes nothing, and the header names those switches.

The bias point

VgsQ, VdsQ and TjQ are needed only when LinearC or one of the four single-capacitance switches is on. Unset with such a switch on, the run stops at its first step with a message naming the switch and the parameters to set.

  • VgsQ and VdsQ are the intrinsic gate–source and drain–source voltages, in V: across the core, inside the network, not at the terminals. They differ from the terminal bias by the drops on the network's resistances.
  • TjQ is the junction temperature at that point, in °C. Unset, it is Temp, and a self-heating device says once that its charge is held at the ambient.

To get them from circuitRF, place the .cmodel as a ComposedFET on the same bias network and run DC. Its intrinsic nodes and its thermal node are in the DC result as X1.gi, X1.di, X1.si and X1.t:

VgsQ = V(X1.gi) − V(X1.si)      VdsQ = V(X1.di) − V(X1.si)      TjQ = temp + V(X1.t)

On the example's bench that is VgsQ = −0.8453, VdsQ = 7.891 and TjQ = 26.36. Or take them from the other simulator's own operating point of the placed module: the same differences across its internal nodes gi, di and si, and the rise on its thermal node ti.

What differs from a ComposedFET

A ComposedFET finds the bias point itself, from the circuit's DC solution; the .va takes it as given. Nothing else differs.

Plots

Every plot is a Data Display plot. Measured traces are symbols and model traces lines. The plots are drawn from the document, so the menu's Plot Properties… and Axes Labels… are greyed; Copy and Export… are always there.

Markers. Double-click a curve, a point or a Smith locus to add a marker. Its info box opens in a band between the plot's title and its axes, beside the boxes already there. Drag a marker to move it along its trace — on the bias plane to the point nearest the pointer — and the arrow keys step it. A bias-plane marker reads its data set and bias. Markers stay through every redraw and reappear when you return to their tab. Select a box and press Delete, or use its menu, to remove one. The Data step's tabs are glyphs: Output and Transfer a small plot marked Vds and Vgs, S one marked S, the bias plane a grid of points, and Smith the Smith glyph. The button at the right of the tab strip, Open in Data Display, sends the plot's data to a new display: the step's plot data, or on the Data, Pads and Network steps the curves the tab shows.

Passive documents: Data and Topology

The Data step lists the block, or the family's blocks with their geometry values, and the analysis lines. The S and Smith tabs show the block's S-parameters.

On the Topology step, Propose ranks the library's topologies against the block and lists the top three, each drawn small with its |ΔS|; double-click one to choose it. A topology of your own is pasted into the network panel. The built-in topologies are one- and two-ports. For a block with more ports, such as a board's six-port EM result, Propose offers nothing unless you draw a topology whose pins 1…N are the ports; the file can also be placed as it is as an S-parameter component.

Undo

Every edit — a value, a lock, a bound, a tie, an exclusion, a step setting, a network choice — is one undo step (⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z). A run is not: it is repeated by running again, and its result stays until the next run replaces it.

From a script or an agent

Every run of this window is a model verb noun — model import, model deembed, model fit, model check-charge, model validate, model export, model report — calling the same function, so a document built in the window runs the same way from a script or an agent. An agent producing the data in another simulator reads Model Data as circuitrf reference model-data, and checks each file with model import --dry-run before anything is written.

References

The primary reference, followed wherever a method choice is open:

  • [P1] J. C. Pedro, D. E. Root, J. Xu, L. C. Nunes, Nonlinear Circuit Simulation and Modeling: Fundamentals for Microwave Design, Cambridge University Press, 2018. Ch. 5: parasitic stripping and the intrinsic linear model. Ch. 6: constitutive relations, tables, ANNs, extrapolation and linearisation (§6.2); charge modeling (§6.3); dispersion (§6.4); symmetry (§6.5); self-heating and trapping (§6.6); waveform-based identification (§6.7).

The papers behind its methods:

Reference Used for
[X03] J. Xu, M. C. E. Yagoub, R. Ding, Q. J. Zhang, "Exact adjoint sensitivity analysis for neural-based microwave modeling and design," IEEE Trans. Microwave Theory Tech., Jan. 2003 The adjoint training of the charges, and value-and-derivative training of Id
[X06] J. Xu, D. Gunyan, M. Iwamoto, A. Cognata, D. E. Root, "Measurement-based non-quasi-static large-signal FET model using artificial neural networks," IEEE MTT-S Int. Microwave Symp., 2006 ANNs over tables where low-level distortion matters; the DC/RF dispersion time constant
[X07] J. Xu, D. Gunyan, M. Iwamoto, J. Horn, A. Cognata, D. E. Root, "Drain-source symmetric artificial neural network-based FET model with robust extrapolation beyond training data," IEEE MTT-S Int. Microwave Symp., 2007 The drain–source symmetry option; guided extrapolation
[X10] J. Xu, J. Horn, M. Iwamoto, D. E. Root, "Large-signal FET model with multiple time scale dynamics from nonlinear vector network analyzer data," IEEE MTT-S Int. Microwave Symp., 2010 Self-heating and trap states as model inputs; temperature in the charges
[X14] J. Xu, R. Jones, S. A. Harris, T. Nielsen, D. E. Root, the GaN dynamic FET model from active source-injection measurements, IEEE MTT-S Int. Microwave Symp., 2014, with its ARFTG (June 2014) validation companion Training on DC, S-parameters and waveforms together; DC I–V as a training target
